Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 3.1)

It’s full of guts and belly,
liver and bladder,
heart and lungs,
kidney and spleen,
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 4.1)

spit and snot,
sweat and fat,
blood and synovial fluid,
bile and grease.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 5.1)

Then in nine streams
the filth is always flowing.
There is muck from the eyes,
wax from the ears,
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 6.1)

and snot from the nostrils.
The mouth sometimes vomits
bile and sometimes phlegm.
And from the body, sweat and waste.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 7.1)

Then there is the hollow head
all filled with brains.
Governed by ignorance,
the fool thinks it’s lovely.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 8.1)

And when it lies dead,
bloated and livid,
dumped in a charnel ground,
the relatives forget it.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 9.1)

It’s devoured by dogs,
by jackals, wolves, and worms.
It’s devoured by crows and vultures,
and any other creatures there.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 10.1)

A wise mendicant here,
having heard the Buddha’s words,
fully understands it,
for they see it as it is.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 11.1)

“As this is, so is that,
as that is, so is this.”
They’d blanch desire for the body
inside and out.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 12.1)

That wise mendicant here
rid of desire and lust,
has found the peace free of death,
extinguishment, the state that does not pass.
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 13.1)

This two-legged body is dirty and stinking,
full of different carcasses,
and oozing all over the place—
but still it is cherished!
Victory Over Desire for the Body (Snp 1.11 14.1)

And if, on account of such a body,
someone prides themselves
or looks down on others—
what is that but a failure to see?
The Sage (Snp 1.12 1.1)

Peril stems from intimacy,
dust comes from an abode.
Freedom from abode and intimacy:
that is the sage’s vision.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 2.1)

Having cut down what’s grown, they wouldn’t replant,
nor would they nurture what’s growing.
That’s who they call a sage wandering alone,
the great seer has seen the state of peace.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 3.1)

Having appraised the fields and measured the seeds,
they wouldn’t nurture them with moisture.
Truly that sage who sees the ending of rebirth
has left speculation behind and is beyond reckoning.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 4.1)

Understanding all the planes of rebirth,
not wanting a single one of them;
truly that sage freed of greed
need not swim, for they have reached the far shore.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 5.1)

The vanquisher of all, knower of all, so very intelligent,
unsullied in the midst of all things,
has given up all, freed in the ending of craving:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 6.1)

Strong in wisdom, with precepts and observances intact,
serene, loving absorption, mindful,
released from chains, kind, undefiled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 7.1)

The diligent sage wandering alone,
is unshaken by blame and praise—
like a lion not startled by sounds,
like wind not caught in a net,
like water not sticking to a lotus.
Leader of others, not by others led:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 8.1)

Steady as a post in a bathing-place
when others speak endlessly against them,
freed of greed, with senses stilled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 9.1)

Steadfast, straight as a spindle,
horrified by wicked deeds,
discerning the just and the unjust:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 10.1)

Restrained, they do no evil,
young or middle-aged, the sage is self-controlled.
Irreproachable, he does not insult anyone:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 11.1)

When one who lives on charity receives alms,
from the top, the middle, or the leftovers,
they think it unworthy to praise or put down:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 12.1)

The sage lives refraining from sex,
even when young is not tied down,
refraining from indulgence and negligence, freed:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 13.1)

Understanding the world, the seer of the ultimate goal,
the unaffected one, having crossed the flood and the ocean,
has cut the ties, unattached and undefiled:
that’s who the attentive know as a sage.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 14.1)

The two are not the same, far apart in lifestyle and conduct—
the householder providing for a wife, and the selfless one true to their vows.
The unrestrained householder kills other creatures,
while the restrained sage always protects living creatures.
The Sage (Snp 1.12 15.1)

As the crested blue-necked peacock flying through the sky
never approaches the speed of the swan,
so the householder cannot compete with the mendicant,
the sage meditating secluded in the woods.
Gems (Snp 2.1 1.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
may beings all be of happy heart,
and listen carefully to what is said.
Gems (Snp 2.1 2.1)

So pay heed, all you beings,
have love for humankind,
who day and night bring offerings;
please protect them diligently.
Gems (Snp 2.1 3.1)

There’s no wealth in this life or the next,
no sublime gem in the heavens,
that equals the Realized One.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 4.1)

Ending, dispassion, the undying, the sublime,
attained by the Sakyan Sage immersed in samādhi;
there is nothing equal to that Dhamma.
This sublime gem is in the Dhamma:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 5.1)

The purity praised by the highest Buddha
is said to be the “immersion with immediate fruit”;
no equal to that immersion is found.
This sublime gem is in the Dhamma:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 6.1)

The eight individual persons praised by the good
are the four pairs of the Holy One’s disciples;
they are worthy of religious donations,
what’s given to them is very fruitful.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 7.1)

Dedicated to Gotama’s dispensation,
strong-minded, free of sense desire,
they’ve attained the goal, plunged into freedom from death,
and enjoy the quenching they’ve freely gained.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 8.1)

As Indra’s pillar rooted in earth
is not shaken by the four winds,
I say a true person is like this,
who sees the noble truths in experience.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 9.1)

Those who fathom the noble truths
taught by the one of deep wisdom,
do not take an eighth life,
even if they are hugely negligent.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 10.1)

When they attain to vision
they give up three things:
substantialist view, doubt, and any
attachment to precepts and observances.
Gems (Snp 2.1 11.1)

They’re freed from the four places of loss,
and cannot do six things.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 12.1)

Even if they do a bad deed
by body, speech, or mind,
they are unable to conceal it;
this, it’s said, is the inability of one who has seen the truth.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 13.1)

Like a tall forest tree crowned with flowers
in the first month of summer;
that’s how he taught the superb Dhamma,
leading to extinguishment, the ultimate benefit.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 14.1)

The superb, knower of the superb, giver of the superb, bringer of the superb;
taught the superb Dhamma supreme.
This sublime gem is in the Buddha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 15.1)

The old is ended, nothing new is produced;
their minds have no desire for future rebirth.
Withered are the seeds, there’s no desire for growth,
those attentive ones are extinguished like this lamp.
This sublime gem is in the Saṅgha:
by this truth, may you be well!
Gems (Snp 2.1 16.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Buddha! May you be safe!
Gems (Snp 2.1 17.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Dhamma! May you be safe!
Gems (Snp 2.1 18.1)

Whatever beings have gathered here,
on the ground or in the sky:
the Realized One is honored by gods and humans!
We bow to the Saṅgha! May you be safe!
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 1.1)

“The good eat properly obtained
millet, wild grains, broomcorn,
greens, tubers, and grapes.
They don’t lie to get what they want.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 2.1)

But when you eat delicious food,
nicely cooked and prepared, and offered by others,
enjoying a dish of fine rice,
Kassapa, you eat putrefaction.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 3.1)

‘Putrefaction is not appropriate for me’—
so you said, O brahmin only by kin.
Yet here you are enjoying a dish of fine rice,
well prepared with the flesh of fowl.
I’m asking you this, Kassapa:
what do you take to be putrefaction?”
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 4.1)

“Killing creatures, mutilation, murder, abduction;
stealing, lying, cheating and fraud,
learning crooked spells, adultery:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 5.1)

People here with unbridled sensuality,
greedy for tastes, mixed up in impurity,
nihilists, immoral, intractable:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 6.1)

Tough, callous calumniators,
pitiless and arrogant betrayers of friends,
misers who never give anything:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 7.1)

Anger, vanity, obstinacy, contrariness,
deceit, jealousy, boastfulness,
haughtiness, intimacy with the wicked:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 8.1)

The ill-behaved, debt-evaders, informants,
business cheats and con-artists,
vile men committing sin:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 9.1)

People here who can’t stop harming living creatures,
taking from others, intent on hurting,
immoral, cruel, harsh, lacking regard for others:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 10.1)

Greedy, hostile, aggressive to others,
and addicted to evil—those beings pass into darkness,
falling headlong into hell:
this is putrefaction, not eating meat.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 11.1)

Not fish or flesh or fasting,
nudity or baldness, or dreadlocks or dirt,
not rough hides or serving the sacred flame,
or the many endless mortifications in the world,
not hymns or oblations, sacrifices or seasonal observances,
will cleanse a mortal not free of doubt.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 12.1)

Guarding the streams of sense impressions, wander with faculties understood,
standing on the teaching, delighting in integrity and tenderness.
The attentive have slipped their chains and given up all suffering;
they don’t cling to the seen and the heard.”
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 13.1)

The Buddha explained this matter to him again and again,
until the master of hymns understood it.
It was illustrated with colorful verses
by the sage free of putrefaction, unattached, hard to trace.
Putrefaction (Snp 2.2 14.1)

Having heard the fine words of the Buddha,
that are free of putrefaction, casting aside all suffering;
humbled, he bowed to the Realized One,
and right away begged to go forth.
Conscientious Companionship (Snp 2.3 1.1)

Flouting conscience, loathing it,
saying “I’m on your side”,
but not following up in deeds—
know they’re not on your side.
Conscientious Companionship (Snp 2.3 2.1)

Some say nice things to their friends
without following it up.
The wise will recognize
one who talks without doing.
Conscientious Companionship (Snp 2.3 3.1)

No true friend relentlessly
suspects betrayal, looking for fault.
One on whom you rest, like a child on the breast,
is a true friend, not split from you by others.
Conscientious Companionship (Snp 2.3 4.1)

One whose reward is the fruit
of bearing the burden of service
develops a happy state,
producing joy and attracting praise.
Conscientious Companionship (Snp 2.3 5.1)

One who has drunk the nectar of seclusion
and the nectar of peace,
free of stress, free of evil,
drinks the joyous nectar of Dhamma.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, late at night, a glorious deity, lighting up the entire Jeta’s Grove, went up to the Buddha, bowed, and stood to one side. That deity addressed the Buddha in verse:
Blessings (Snp 2.4 2.1)

“Many gods and humans
have thought about blessings
desiring well-being:
declare the highest blessing.”
Blessings (Snp 2.4 3.1)

“Not to fraternize with fools,
but to fraternize with the wise,
and honoring those worthy of honor:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 4.1)

Living in a suitable region,
having made merit in the past,
being rightly resolved in oneself,
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 5.1)

Education and a craft,
discipline and training,
and well-spoken speech:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 6.1)

Caring for mother and father,
kindness to children and partners,
and unstressful work:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 7.1)

Giving and righteous conduct,
kindness to relatives,
blameless deeds:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 8.1)

Desisting and abstaining from evil,
avoiding drinking liquor,
diligence in good qualities:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 9.1)

Respect and placidity,
contentment and gratitude,
and timely listening to the teaching:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 10.1)

Patience, being easy to admonish,
the sight of ascetics,
and timely discussion of the teaching:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 11.1)

Fervor and chastity
seeing the noble truths,
and realization of extinguishment:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 12.1)

Though touched by worldly conditions,
their mind does not tremble;
sorrowless, stainless, secure:
this is the highest blessing.
Blessings (Snp 2.4 13.1)

Having completed these things,
undefeated everywhere;
everywhere they go in safety:
this is their highest blessing.”
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Gayā on the cut-stone ledge in the haunt of Spiky the native spirit. Now at that time the native spirits Shaggy and Spiky were passing by not far from the Buddha. So Shaggy said to Spiky, “That’s an ascetic.” “That’s no ascetic, he’s a faker! I’ll soon find out whether he’s an ascetic or a faker.”
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 2.1)

Then Spiky went up to the Buddha and leaned up against his body, but the Buddha pulled away. Then Spiky said to the Buddha, “Are you afraid, ascetic?” “No, respectable sir, I’m not afraid. But your touch is nasty.”
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 3.1)
“I will ask you a question, ascetic. If you don’t answer me, I’ll drive you insane, or explode your heart, or grab you by the feet and throw you to the far shore of the Ganges!”
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 4.1)

“I don’t see anyone in this world with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans who could do that to me. But anyway, ask what you wish.” Then Spiky addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 5.1)

“Where do greed and hate come from?
From where spring discontent, desire, and terror?
Where do the mind’s thoughts originate,
like a crow let loose by boys.”
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 6.1)
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 7.1)

Born of affection, originating in oneself,
like prop roots sprouting from a banyan;
the many kinds of attachment to sensual pleasures
are like camel’s foot creeper creeping through the woods.
With Spiky (Snp 2.5 8.1)

Those who understand where they come from
dispel them—listen up, spirit!
They cross this flood so hard to cross,
not crossed before, so as to not be reborn.”
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 1.1)

A righteous life, a spiritual life,
they call this the supreme treasure.
But if someone goes forth
from the lay life to homelessness
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 2.1)

who is of scurrilous character,
a beast and a bully,
their life gets worse,
as poison grows inside them.
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 3.1)

A mendicant who loves to quarrel,
wrapped in delusion,
doesn’t even know what’s been explained
in the Dhamma taught by the Buddha.
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 4.1)

Harassing those who are evolved,
governed by ignorance,
they don’t know that corruption
is the path that leads to hell.
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 5.1)

Entering the underworld,
passing from womb to womb, from darkness to darkness,
such a mendicant
falls into suffering after death.
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 6.1)

One such as that is
like a sewer
brimful with years of filth
for it’s hard to clean one full of grime.
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 7.1)

Mendicants, knowing that someone is like this,
attached to the domestic life,
of corrupt wishes and wicked intent,
of bad behavior and alms-resort,
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 8.1)

then having gathered in harmony,
you should expel them.
Throw out the trash!
Get rid of the rubbish!
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 9.1)

And sweep away the scraps—
they’re not ascetics, they just think they are.
When you’ve thrown out those of corrupt wishes,
of bad behavior and alms-resort,
A Righteous Life (Snp 2.6 10.1)

dwell in communion, ever mindful,
the pure with the pure.
Then in harmony, alert,
you’ll make an end of suffering.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then several old and well-to-do brahmins of Kosala—elderly and senior, who were advanced in years and had reached the final stage of life—went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, they sat down to one side and said to the Buddha: “Worthy Gotama, are the ancient principles of the brahmins exhibited these days among brahmins?” “No, brahmins, they are not.” “If you wouldn’t mind, Worthy Gotama, please teach us the ancient principles of the brahmins.” “Well then, brahmins, listen and apply your mind well, I will speak.” “Yes, worthy sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 2.1)

“The ancient seers used to be
restrained and austere.
Having given up the five sensual stimuli,
they lived for their own true good.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 3.1)

Brahmins used to own no cattle,
nor gold coin or grain.
Chanting was their money and grain,
which they guarded as a gift from god.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 4.1)

Food was prepared for them
and left beside their doors.
People believed that food prepared in faith
should be given to them.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 5.1)

With colorful clothes,
lodgings and houses,
prosperous nations and countries
honored those brahmins.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 6.1)

Brahmins used to be inviolable and
invincible, protected by principle.
No one ever turned them away
from the doors of families.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 7.1)

For forty-eight years
they led the spiritual life.
The brahmins of old pursued
their quest for knowledge and conduct.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 8.1)

Brahmins never transgressed with another,
nor did they purchase a wife.
They lived together in love,
joining together by mutual consent.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 9.1)

Brahmins never approached their wives for sex
during the time outside
the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle
after menstruation.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 10.1)

They praised chastity and morality,
integrity, tenderness, and fervor,
gentleness and harmlessness,
and also patience.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 11.1)

He who was supreme among them,
godlike, staunchly vigorous,
did not engage in sex
even in a dream.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 12.1)

Training in line with their duties,
many smart people here
praised chastity and morality,
and also patience.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 13.1)

They begged for rice,
bedding, clothes, ghee, and oil.
Having collected them legitimately,
they arranged a sacrifice.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 14.1)

But they slew no cows
while serving at the sacrifice.
Like a mother, father, or brother,
or some other relative,
cows are our best friends,
the fonts of medicine.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 15.1)

They give food and strength,
and beauty and happiness.
Knowing these benefits,
they slew no cows.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 16.1)

The brahmins were delicate and tall,
beautiful and glorious.
They were keen on all the duties
according to their teachings.
So long as they continued in the world,
people flourished happily.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 17.1)

But perversion crept into them
little by little when they saw
the transformation of the king
and the ladies in all their finery.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 18.1)

Their chariots were harnessed with thoroughbreds,
well-made with bright canopies,
and their homes and houses
were neatly divided section by section.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 19.1)

They were lavished with herds of cattle,
and furnished with bevies of lovely ladies.
This extravagant human wealth
was coveted by the brahmins.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 20.1)

They compiled hymns to that end,
approached King Okkāka and said,
‘You have plenty of money and grain.
Sacrifice! For you have much treasure.
Sacrifice! For you have much money.’
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 21.1)

Persuaded by the brahmins,
the king, chief of charioteers, performed
horse sacrifice, human sacrifice,
the sacrifices of the ‘casting of the yoke-pin’, the ‘royal soma drinking’, and the ‘unimpeded’.
When he had carried out these sacrifices,
he gave riches to the brahmins.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 22.1)
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 23.1)

and lovely homes,
nicely divided section by section.
Having furnished them with different grains,
he gave riches to the brahmins.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 24.1)

When they got hold of that wealth,
they arranged to store it up.
Falling under the sway of desire,
their craving grew and grew.
They compiled hymns to that end,
approached King Okkāka once more and said,
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 25.1)

‘Like water and earth,
gold coin, riches, and grain,
are cows for humankind,
as they are essential for creatures.
Sacrifice! For you have much treasure.
Sacrifice! For you have much money.’
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 26.1)

Persuaded by the brahmins,
the king, chief of charioteers,
had many hundred thousand cows
slain at the sacrifice.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 27.1)

Neither with feet nor with horns
do cows harm anyone at all.
Cows meek as lambs
supply buckets of milk.
But taking them by the horns,
the king slew them with a sword.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 28.1)

At that the gods and the ancestors,
with Indra, the titans and monsters,
roared out: ‘This is a crime against nature!’
as the sword fell on the cows.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 29.1)

There used to be three kinds of illness:
greed, starvation, and old age.
But due to the slaughter of cows,
this grew to be ninety-eight.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 30.1)

This crime of the rods
is of ancient descent.
Killing innocent creatures,
the sacrificers forsake righteousness.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 31.1)

And that is how this mean old practice
was criticized by sensible people.
Wherever they see such a thing,
folk criticize the sacrificer.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 32.1)

With righteousness gone,
peasants and menials were split,
as were many aristocrats,
and wives looked down on their husbands.
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 33.1)

Aristocrats and brahmins only by kin,
and others protected by their clan,
neglecting their genealogy,
fell under the sway of sensual pleasures.”
Brahmanical Principles (Snp 2.7 34.1)

When he had spoken, those well-to-do brahmins said to the Buddha, “Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember us as lay followers who have gone for refuge for life.”
The Boat (Snp 2.8 1.1)

If you would learn the teaching from someone,
honor them as the gods honor Indra.
Then they will have confidence in you,
and being learned, they reveal the teaching.
The Boat (Snp 2.8 2.1)

Heeding well, an attentive one,
practicing in line with that teaching
grows intelligent, discerning, and subtle
through diligently sticking close to such a person.
The Boat (Snp 2.8 3.1)

But associating with a petty fool
who falls short of the goal, jealous,
then unable to discern the teaching in this life,
one proceeds to death still plagued by doubts.
The Boat (Snp 2.8 4.1)

It’s like a man who has plunged into a river,
a rushing torrent in spate.
As they are swept away downstream,
how could they help others across?
The Boat (Snp 2.8 5.1)

Just so, one unable to discern the teaching,
who hasn’t studied the meaning under the learned,
not knowing it oneself, still plagued by doubts,
how could they help others to contemplate?
The Boat (Snp 2.8 6.1)

But one who has embarked on a strong boat
equipped with rudder and oar,
would bring many others across there
with skill, care, and thoughtfulness.
The Boat (Snp 2.8 7.1)

So too one who understands—a knowledge master,
evolved, learned, and unflappable—
can help others to contemplate,
so long as they are prepared to listen carefully.
The Boat (Snp 2.8 8.1)

That’s why you should spend time with a true person,
intelligent and learned.
Having understood the meaning, putting it into practice,
one who understands the teaching would find happiness.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 1.1)

“With what morality, what conduct,
fostering what deeds,
would a person lay the foundations right,
and reach the highest goal?”
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 2.1)

“Honoring elders without jealousy,
they’d know the time to visit their respected teachers.
Treasuring the chance for a Dhamma talk,
they’d listen carefully to the well-spoken words.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 3.1)

At the right time, they’d enter the vicinity of their respected teachers
in placid manner, leaving obstinacy behind.
They’d call to mind and put into practice
the meaning, the teaching, self-control, and the spiritual life.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 4.1)

Delighting in the teaching, enjoying the teaching,
standing on the teaching, evaluating the teaching,
they’d never say anything that degraded the teaching,
but would be guided by genuine words well-spoken.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 5.1)

Giving up mirth, muttered prayer, weeping, ill will,
deceit, fawning, greed, conceit,
aggression, crudeness, stains, and indulgence,
they’d wander free of vanity, steadfast.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 6.1)

Understanding is the essence of well-spoken words,
stillness is the essence of learning and understanding.
Wisdom and learning do not flourish
in a hasty and negligent person.
What Morality? (Snp 2.9 7.1)

Those happy with the teaching proclaimed by the Noble One
are supreme in speech, mind, and deed.
Abiding in peace, gentleness, and stillness,
they’ve realized the essence of learning and wisdom.”
Get Up! (Snp 2.10 1.1)

Get up and meditate!
What’s the point in your sleeping?
How can the afflicted slumber
when inflicted by an arrow strike?
Get Up! (Snp 2.10 2.1)

Get up and meditate!
Train hard for peace!
The King of Death has caught you heedless—
don’t let him fool you under his sway.
Get Up! (Snp 2.10 3.1)

Needy gods and humans
are held back by clinging:
get over it.
Don’t let the moment pass you by.
For if you miss your moment
you’ll grieve when sent to hell.
Get Up! (Snp 2.10 4.1)

Negligence is always dust;
dust follows right behind negligence.
Through diligence and knowledge,
pluck out the dart from yourself.
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 1.1)

“Does familiarity breed contempt,
even for the man of wisdom?
Do you honor he who holds aloft
the torch for all humanity?”
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 2.1)

“Familiarity breeds no contempt
for the man of wisdom.
I always honor he who holds aloft
the torch for all humanity.”
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 3.1)

“One who’s given up the five sensual stimulations,
so pleasing and delightful,
and who’s left the home life out of faith—
let them make an end to suffering!
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 4.1)

Mix with spiritual friends,
stay in remote lodgings,
secluded and quiet,
and eat in moderation.
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 5.1)

Robes, almsfood,
requisites and lodgings:
don’t crave such things;
don’t come back to this world again.
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 6.1)

Be restrained in the monastic code
and the five sense faculties.
With mindfulness immersed in the body,
be full of disillusionment.
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 7.1)

Turn away from the sign
that’s attractive, provoking lust.
With mind unified and serene,
meditate on the ugly aspects of the body.
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 8.1)

Meditate on the signless,
give up the tendency to conceit;
and when you comprehend conceit,
you will live at peace.”
With Rāhula (Snp 2.11 9.1)
That is how the Buddha regularly advised Venerable Rāhula with these verses.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Āḷavī, at Āḷavī’s premier shrine. Now at that time it was not long after Venerable Vaṅgīsa’s mentor, the senior monk named Nigrodhakappa, had become fully quenched. Then as Vaṅgīsa was in private retreat this thought came to his mind: “Has my mentor become quenched or not?” Then in the late afternoon, Venerable Vaṅgīsa came out of retreat and went to the Buddha. He bowed, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Just now, sir, as I was in private retreat this thought came to mind. ‘Has my mentor become quenched or not?’” Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him in verse:
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 2.1)

“I ask the Teacher unrivaled in wisdom,
who has cut off all doubts in this very life:
a monk has died at Āḷavī’s premier shrine,
who was well-known, famous, and quenched.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 3.1)

Nigrodhakappa was his name;
it was given to that brahmin by you, Blessed One.
He wandered in your honor, yearning for freedom,
energetic, a resolute Seer of Truth.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 4.1)

O Sakyan, All-seer,
we all wish to know about that disciple.
Our ears are eager to hear,
for you are the most excellent teacher.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 5.1)

Cut off our doubt, declare this to us;
your wisdom is vast, tell us of his quenching!
All-seer, speak among us,
like the thousand-eyed Sakka in the midst of the gods!
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 6.1)

Whatever ties there are, or paths to delusion,
or things on the side of unknowing, or that are bases of doubt
vanish on reaching a Realized One,
for his eye is the best of all people’s.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 7.1)

If no man were ever to disperse corruptions,
like the wind dispersing the stormclouds,
darkness would shroud the whole world;
not even brilliant men would shine.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 8.1)

The attentive are bringers of light;
my hero, that is what I think of you.
We’ve come for your discernment and knowledge:
here in this assembly, declare to us about Kappāyana.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 9.1)

Swiftly send forth your sweet, sweet voice,
like a goose stretching its neck, gently honking,
lucid-flowing, with lovely tone:
alert, we all listen to you.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 10.1)

You have entirely abandoned birth and death;
curbed and pure, I urge you, speak the Dhamma!
For ordinary people have no wish-granter,
but Realized Ones have a comprehensibility-granter.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 11.1)

Your answer is definitive, and we will adopt it,
for you have perfect understanding.
We raise our cupped palms one last time,
one of unrivaled wisdom, don’t deliberately confuse us.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 12.1)

Knowing the teaching of the noble ones from top to bottom,
one of unrivaled energy, don’t deliberately confuse us.
As a man baking in the summer sun would long for water,
I long for your voice, so let the sound rain forth.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 13.1)

Surely Kappāyana did not lead the spiritual life in vain?
Did he realize quenching,
or did he still have a residue?
Let us hear what kind of liberation he had!”
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 14.1)

“He cut off craving for name and form right here,” said the Buddha,
“the river of darkness that had long lain within him.
He has entirely crossed over birth and death.”
So declared the Blessed One, the leader of the five.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 15.1)

“Now that I have heard your words,
seventh of seers, I am confident.
My question, it seems, was not in vain,
the brahmin did not deceive me.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 16.1)

As he said, so he did—
he was a disciple of the Buddha.
He cut the net of death the deceiver,
so extended and strong.
Vaṅgīsa and His Mentor Nigrodhakappa (Snp 2.12 17.1)

Blessed One, Kappāyana saw
the starting point of grasping.
He has indeed gone far beyond
Death’s dominion so hard to pass.”
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 1.1)

“I ask the sage abounding in wisdom—
crossed-over, gone beyond, quenched, steadfast:
when a mendicant has left home, casting aside sensuality,
what’s the right way to wander the world?”
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 2.1)

“When they’ve eradicated superstitions,” said the Buddha,
“about celestial portents, dreams, or bodily marks;
with the stain of superstitions left behind,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 3.1)

A mendicant ought dispel desire
for pleasures human or heavenly;
with rebirth transcended and truth comprehended,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 4.1)

Putting backbiting behind them,
a mendicant gives up anger and stinginess;
with favoring and opposing left behind,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 5.1)

When the loved and the unloved are both left behind,
not grasping or dependent on anything;
freed from all things that fetter,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 6.1)

Finding no core in attachments,
rid of desire for things they’ve acquired,
independent, needing no one to guide them,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 7.1)

Not hostile in speech, mind, or deed,
they’ve rightly understood the teaching.
Aspiring to the state of extinguishment,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 8.1)
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 9.1)

When greed and craving to live again are cast off,
a mendicant refrains from violence and abduction;
rid of indecision, free of thorns,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 10.1)

Knowing what is suitable for themselves,
a mendicant would hurt no one in the world;
understanding the teaching in line with the truth,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 11.1)

They have no underlying tendencies at all,
and are rid of unskillful roots;
free of hope, with no need for hope,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 12.1)

Defilements ended, conceit given up,
beyond all manner of desire;
tamed, quenched, and steadfast,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 13.1)

Faithful, learned, seer of the sure path,
an attentive one joins no faction among sects;
rid of greed, hate, and aversion,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 14.1)

A purified victor with veil cast off,
among worldly things master, transcendent, stilled;
expert in knowledge of conditions’ cessation,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 15.1)

They’re over speculating on the future or past,
and understand what it means to be pure;
freed from all the sense fields,
they’d rightly wander the world.
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 16.1)

The state of peace is understood, the truth is comprehended,
they’ve openly seen defilements cast off;
and with the ending of all attachments,
they’d rightly wander the world.”
The Right Way to Wander (Snp 2.13 17.1)

“Clearly, Blessed One, it is just as you say.
One who lives like this is a tamed mendicant,
passed beyond all fetters and yokes:
they’d rightly wander the world.”
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the lay follower Dhammika, together with five hundred lay followers, went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and addressed him in verse:
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 2.1)

“I ask you, Gotama, whose wisdom is vast:
what does one do to become a good disciple,
both one who has left the home,
and the lay followers staying at home?
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 3.1)

For you understand the course and destiny
of the world with all its gods.
There is no equal to you who sees the subtle meaning,
for you are the Buddha most excellent, they say.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 4.1)

Having experienced all knowledge,
you reveal the teaching out of sympathy for beings.
All-seer, you have cast off the veil,
and immaculate, you dazzle the whole world.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 5.1)

The dragon king Erāvaṇa, hearing you called ‘Victor’,
came into your presence.
He consulted with you then, having heard your words,
left consoled, saying ‘Excellent!’
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 6.1)

And King Kuvera Vessavaṇa also
approached to ask about the teaching.
You also answered him, O attentive one,
and hearing you he too was consoled.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 7.1)

Those monastics of other religions given to debate,
whether Ājīvakas or Jains,
all fail to overtake you in wisdom,
like a standing man next to a sprinter.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 8.1)

Those brahmins given to debate,
some of whom are quite senior,
all end up beholden to you for the meaning,
and others too who think themselves debaters.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 9.1)

So subtle and pleasant is the teaching
that is well proclaimed by you, Blessed One.
It’s all we long to hear. So when asked,
O Best of Buddhas, tell us!
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 10.1)

All these mendicants have gathered,
and the layfolk too are here to listen.
Let them hear the teaching the immaculate one discovered,
like gods listening to the fine words of Vāsava.”
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 11.1)

“Listen to me, mendicants, I will educate you
in the cleansing teaching; all bear it in mind.
A thoughtful person, seeing the meaning,
would adopt the deportment proper to a renunciate.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 12.1)

No way would a mendicant go out at the wrong time;
at the right time, they’d walk the village for alms.
For chains bind one who wanders at the wrong time,
which is why the Buddhas avoid it.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 13.1)

Sights, sounds, tastes, smells, and touches,
which drive beings mad—
dispel desire for such things,
and enter for the morning meal at the right time.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 14.1)

After receiving alms for the day,
on returning a mendicant would sit in private alone.
Inwardly reflective, they’d curb their mind
from outside things, keeping themselves collected.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 15.1)

Should they converse with a disciple,
with anyone else, or with a mendicant,
they’d bring up only the sublime teaching,
not dividing or blaming.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 16.1)

For some contend in debate,
but we praise not those of little wisdom.
In place after place they are bound in chains,
for they send their mind over there far away.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 17.1)

Alms, a dwelling, a bed and seat,
and water for rinsing the dust from the cloak—
after hearing the teaching of the Holy One,
a disciple of outstanding wisdom would use these after appraisal.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 18.1)

That’s why, when it comes to alms and lodgings,
and water for rinsing the dust from the cloak,
a mendicant is unsullied in the midst of these things,
like a droplet on a lotus-leaf.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 19.1)

Now I shall tell you the householder’s duty,
doing which one becomes a good disciple.
For one burdened with possessions does not get to realize
the whole of the mendicant’s practice.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 20.1)

They’d not kill any creature, nor have them killed,
nor grant permission for others to kill.
They’ve laid aside violence toward all creatures
frail or firm that there are in the world.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 21.1)

Next, a disciple would avoid knowingly
taking anything not given at all,
they’d not get others to do it, nor grant them permission to steal;
they’d avoid all theft.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 22.1)

A sensible person would avoid the unchaste life,
like a burning pit of coals.
But if unable to remain chaste,
they’d not transgress with another’s partner.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 23.1)

In a council or assembly,
or one on one, they would not lie.
They’d not get others to lie, nor grant them permission to lie;
they’d avoid all untruths.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 24.1)

A householder espousing this teaching
would not consume liquor or drink.
They’d not get others to drink, nor grant them permission to drink;
knowing that ends in intoxication.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 25.1)

For drunken fools do bad things,
and encourage other heedless folk.
Shun this field of demerit,
the maddening, deluding frolic of fools.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 26.1)

You shouldn’t kill living creatures, or steal,
or lie, or drink liquor.
Be chaste, refraining from sex,
and don’t eat at night, the wrong time.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 27.1)

Not wearing garlands or applying fragrance,
you should sleep on a low bed, or a mat on the ground.
This is the eight-factored sabbath, they say,
revealed by the Buddha, who has gone to suffering’s end.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 28.1)

Then having rightly undertaken the sabbath
complete in all its eight factors
on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth of the fortnight,
as well as on the fortnightly special displays,
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 29.1)

at daybreak after the sabbath
a clever person, rejoicing with confident heart,
would distribute food and drink
to the mendicant Saṅgha as is fitting.
With Dhammika (Snp 2.14 30.1)

One should rightfully support one’s parents,
and undertake a legitimate business.
A diligent layperson observing these duties
ascends to the gods named ‘self-radiant’.”
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 1.1)

“I shall extol going forth
with the example of the Clear-eyed One,
the course of inquiry that led to
his choice to go forth.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 2.1)

‘This life at home is cramped,
a realm of dirt.’
‘The life of one gone forth is like an open space.’
Seeing this, he went forth.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 3.1)

Having gone forth, he shunned
bad deeds of body.
And leaving verbal misconduct behind,
he purified his livelihood.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 4.1)

The Buddha went to Rājagaha,
the Mountainfold of the Magadhans.
He betook himself for alms,
replete with excellent marks.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 5.1)

Bimbisāra saw him
while standing atop his longhouse.
Noticing that he was endowed with marks,
he said the following:
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 6.1)

‘Pay heed, sirs, to this one,
handsome, majestic, radiant;
accomplished in deportment,
he looks just a plough’s length in front.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 7.1)

Eyes downcast, mindful,
unlike one from a low family.
Let the king’s messengers run out,
and find where the mendicant will go.’
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 8.1)

The messengers sent out
followed right behind, thinking
‘Where will the mendicant go?
Where shall he find a place to stay?’
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 9.1)

Wandering indiscriminately for alms,
sense doors guarded and well restrained,
aware and mindful,
his bowl was quickly filled.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 10.1)

Having wandered for alms,
the sage left the city.
He betook himself to Mount Paṇḍava,
thinking, ‘Here is the place I shall stay.’
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 11.1)

Seeing that he had arrived at a place to stay,
the messengers withdrew nearby,
but one of them returned
to inform the king.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 12.1)

‘Great king, the mendicant
is on the east flank of Mount Paṇḍava.
There he sits, like a tiger or a bull,
like a lion in a mountain cave.’
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 13.1)

Hearing the messenger’s report,
the aristocrat set out
hurriedly in his fine chariot
toward Mount Paṇḍava.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 14.1)

He went as far as vehicles could go,
then dismounted from his chariot,
approached on foot,
and reaching him, drew near.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 15.1)

Seated, the king greeted him
and made polite conversation.
When the courtesies were over,
he said the following:
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 16.1)

‘You are young, just a youth,
a lad in the prime of life.
You are endowed with beauty and stature,
like an aristocrat of good birth
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 17.1)

in glory at the army’s head,
surrounded by a troop of elephants.
I offer you pleasures—enjoy them!
But please tell me of your birth.’
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 18.1)

‘Up north, O King,
on the slopes of the Himalayas,
full of wealth and strength, lies the land
of one whose abode is among the Kosalans.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 19.1)

Their clan is named for the Sun,
they are Sakyans by birth.
I have gone forth from that family—
I do not yearn for sensual pleasure.
Going Forth (Snp 3.1 20.1)

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,
seeing renunciation as sanctuary,
I shall go on to strive;
that is where my mind delights.’”
Striving (Snp 3.2 1.1)

“During my time of resolute striving
back on the bank of the Nerañjara River,
I was meditating very hard
for the sake of sanctuary from the yoke.
Striving (Snp 3.2 2.1)

Namucī approached,
speaking words of kindness:
‘You’re thin, discolored,
on the verge of death.
Striving (Snp 3.2 3.1)

Death has a thousand parts of you,
one fraction is left to life.
Live, worthy sir! Life is better!
Living, you can make merits.
Striving (Snp 3.2 4.1)

While leading the spiritual life
and serving the sacred flame,
you can pile up abundant merit—
so what will striving do for you?
Striving (Snp 3.2 5.1)

Hard to walk is the path of striving,
hard to do, a hard challenge to win.’”
These are the verses Māra spoke
as he stood beside the Buddha.
Striving (Snp 3.2 6.1)

When Māra had spoken in this way,
the Buddha said this:
“O Wicked One, kinsman of the negligent,
you’re here for your own purpose.
Striving (Snp 3.2 7.1)

I have no need for
the slightest bit of merit.
Those with need for merit
are fit for Māra to address.
Striving (Snp 3.2 8.1)

I have faith and energy too,
and wisdom is found in me.
When I am so resolute,
why do you beg me to live?
Striving (Snp 3.2 9.1)

The rivers and streams
might be dried by the wind,
so why, when I am resolute,
should it not dry up my blood?
Striving (Snp 3.2 10.1)

And while the blood is drying up,
the bile and phlegm dry too.
And as my muscles waste away,
my mind grows more serene.
And all the stronger grow mindfulness
and wisdom and immersion.
Striving (Snp 3.2 11.1)

As I meditate like this,
having attained the supreme feeling,
my mind has no interest in sensual pleasures:
behold a being’s purity!
Striving (Snp 3.2 12.1)

Sensual pleasures are your first army,
the second is called discontent,
hunger and thirst are the third,
and the fourth is said to be craving.
Striving (Snp 3.2 13.1)

Your fifth is dullness and drowsiness,
the sixth is said to be cowardice,
your seventh is doubt,
contempt and obstinacy are your eighth.
Striving (Snp 3.2 14.1)

Profit, praise, and honor,
and misbegotten fame;
the extolling of oneself
while scorning others.
Striving (Snp 3.2 15.1)

This is your army, Namucī,
the strike force of the Dark One.
Only a hero can defeat it,
but in victory there lies bliss.
Striving (Snp 3.2 16.1)

Let me gird myself—
curse my life!
I’d rather die in battle
than live on in defeat.
Striving (Snp 3.2 17.1)

Here some ascetics and brahmins
are swallowed up, not to be seen again.
And they do not know the path
traveled by those true to their vows.
Striving (Snp 3.2 18.1)

Seeing Māra ready with his legions,
surrounded by his bannered forces,
I shall meet them in battle—
they’ll never make me retreat!
Striving (Snp 3.2 19.1)

That army of yours has never been beaten
by the world with all its gods.
Yet I shall smash it with wisdom,
like an unfired pot with a stone.
Striving (Snp 3.2 20.1)

Having brought my thoughts under control,
and established mindfulness well,
I shall wander from nation to nation,
guiding many disciples.
Striving (Snp 3.2 21.1)

Diligent and resolute,
following my instructions,
they will proceed despite your will,
to where there is no sorrow.”
Striving (Snp 3.2 22.1)

“For seven years I followed
step by step behind the Blessed One.
I found no vulnerability
in the mindful Awakened One.
Striving (Snp 3.2 23.1)

A crow once circled a stone
that looked like a lump of fat.
‘Perhaps I’ll find something tender,’ it thought,
‘perhaps there’s something tasty.’
Striving (Snp 3.2 24.1)

But finding nothing tasty,
the crow left that place.
Like the crow that pecked the stone,
I leave Gotama disappointed.”
Striving (Snp 3.2 25.1)

So stricken with sorrow
that his harp dropped from his armpit,
that spirit, downcast,
vanished right there.
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Buddha addressed the mendicants, “Mendicants!” “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Buddha said this:
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 2.1)

“Mendicants, speech that has four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It’s blameless and is not criticized by sensible people. What four? It’s when a mendicant speaks well, not poorly; their speech is principled, not unprincipled; they speak pleasantly, not unpleasantly; and they speak truthfully, not falsely. Speech with these four factors is well spoken, not poorly spoken. It’s blameless and is not criticized by sensible people.” That is what the Buddha said. Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 3.1)
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 4.1)

Then Venerable Vaṅgīsa rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and said, “I feel inspired to speak, Blessed One! I feel inspired to speak, Holy One!” “Then speak as you feel inspired,” said the Buddha. Then Vaṅgīsa extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 5.1)

“Speak only those words
that do not hurt yourself
nor harm others;
such speech is truly well spoken.
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 6.1)

Speak only pleasing words,
words gladly welcomed.
Pleasing words are those
that bring nothing bad to others.
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 7.1)

Truth itself is undying speech:
this is an ancient teaching.
Good people say the teaching and meaning
are grounded in truth.
Well-Spoken Words (Snp 3.3 8.1)
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying in the Kosalan lands on the bank of the Sundarikā River. Now at that time the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā was serving the sacred flame and performing the fire sacrifice on the bank of the Sundarikā. Then he rose from his seat and surveyed the four quarters, wondering, “Now who might eat the leftovers of this oblation?” He saw the Buddha meditating at the root of a certain tree with his robe pulled over his head. Taking the leftovers of the oblation in his left hand and a pitcher in the right he approached the Buddha.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 2.1)

When he heard Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā’s footsteps the Buddha uncovered his head. Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā thought, “This man is shaven, he is shaven!” And he wanted to turn back. But he thought, “Even some brahmins are shaven. Why don’t I go to him and ask about his birth?” Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā went up to the Buddha, and said to him, “Sir, what are you by birth?”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 3.1)
Then the Buddha addressed Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā in verse:
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 4.1)

“I am no brahmin, nor am I a ruler,
nor peasant nor anything else.
Fully understanding the clan of ordinary people,
I wander in the world owning nothing, reflective.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 5.1)

Clad in my cloak, I wander without home,
my hair shorn, quenched.
Since I’m unburdened by sons of Manu,
it’s inappropriate to ask me about clan.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 6.1)

“Actually sir, when brahmins meet they politely
ask each other whether they are brahmins.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 7.1)

“Well, if you say that you’re a brahmin,
and that I am not,
I shall question you on that Sāvitrī Prayer,
with its three lines and twenty-four syllables.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 8.1)

“On what grounds have seers and men,
aristocrats and brahmins here in the world
performed so many different sacrifices to the gods?”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 9.1)

“During a sacrifice, should a past-master, a knowledge master,
receive an oblation, it profits the donor, I say.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 10.1)

“Then clearly my oblation will be profitable,” said the brahmin,
“since I have met such a knowledge master.
It’s because I’d never met anyone like you
that others ate the sacrificial cake.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 11.1)

“So then, brahmin, since you have approached me
as a seeker of the good, ask.
Perhaps you may find here someone intelligent,
peaceful, unclouded, untroubled, with no need for hope.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 12.1)

“Worthy Gotama, I like to sacrifice
and wish to perform a sacrifice. Please advise me,
for I do not understand
where an oblation is profitable; tell me this.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 13.1)
“Well then, brahmin, listen up, I will teach you the Dhamma.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 14.1)

Don’t ask about birth, ask about conduct;
for the fire of Jātaveda is born from sticks.
A steadfast sage, even though from a low class family,
is a thoroughbred checked by conscience.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 15.1)

Tamed by truth, fulfilled by taming,
a complete knowledge master who has completed the spiritual journey—
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 16.1)

Those who have left sensuality behind, wandering homeless,
self-controlled, straight as a shuttle—
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 17.1)

Those freed of greed, with senses stilled,
like the moon released from the eclipse—
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 18.1)

They wander the world unobstructed,
always mindful, calling nothing their own—
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 19.1)

Having left sensuality behind, wandering triumphant,
knowing the end of rebirth and death,
quenched and cool as a lake:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 20.1)

Good among the good, far from the bad,
the Realized One has infinite wisdom.
Unsullied in this life and the next:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 21.1)

In whom dwells no deceit or conceit,
rid of greed, unselfish, with no need for hope,
with anger cast aside, quenched,
a brahmin rid of sorrow’s stain:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 22.1)

He has given up the mind’s home,
and has no possessions at all.
Not grasping to this life or the next:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 23.1)

Serene, he has crossed the flood,
and has understood the teaching with ultimate view.
With defilements ended, bearing his final body:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 24.1)

In whom desire to be reborn, and caustic speech
are cleared and ended, and are no more;
that knowledge master, everywhere free:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 25.1)

He has slipped his chains, he’s chained no more,
among those caught in conceit he is free of conceit;
he has fully understood suffering with its field and ground:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 26.1)

Not relying on hope, seeing seclusion,
well past the views proclaimed by others.
In him there are no supporting conditions at all:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 27.1)

He has comprehended all things, high and low,
cleared them and ended them, so they are no more.
Peaceful, freed in the ending of grasping:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 28.1)

He sees the ending of rebirth’s fetter,
and has cast aside all manner of desire.
Pure, stainless, immaculate, flawless:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 29.1)

Not seeing himself in terms of a self,
he is stilled, sincere, and steadfast.
Imperturbable, kind, wishless:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 30.1)

He harbors no delusions within at all,
he has insight into all things.
He bears his final body,
attained to the state of grace, the supreme awakening.
That’s how the purity of a spirit is defined:
the Realized One is worthy of the sacrificial cake.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 31.1)

“Let my oblation be a true offering,
since I have found such a knowledge master!
I see divinity in person! Accept my offering, Blessed One:
please eat my sacrificial cake.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 32.1)

“Food enchanted by a verse isn’t fit for me to eat.
That’s not the principle of those who see, brahmin.
The Buddhas cast aside things enchanted with verses.
Since there is such a principle, brahmin, that’s how they live.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 33.1)

Serve with other food and drink
the consummate one, the great seer,
with defilements ended and remorse stilled.
For he is the field for the seeker of merit.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 34.1)

“Please, Blessed One, help me understand:
now that I have found your teaching,
when I look for someone during a sacrifice,
who should eat the religious donation of one like me?”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 35.1)

“One who is rid of aggression,
whose mind is unclouded,
who is liberated from sensual pleasures,
and who has cast aside dullness.
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 36.1)

One who has erased perimeters and limits,
expert in birth and death,
a sage, blessed with sagacity.
When such a person comes to the sacrifice,
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 37.1)

get rid of your scowl!
Honor them with cupped palms,
and venerate them with food and drink,
and in this way your religious donation will succeed.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 38.1)

“The Buddha is worthy of the sacrificial cake,
he is the supreme field of merit,
recipient of gifts from the whole world;
what’s given to the worthy one is very fruitful.”
With Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā on the Sacrificial Cake (Snp 3.4 39.1)

Then the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā said to the Buddha, “Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! As if he were righting the overturned, or revealing the hidden, or pointing out the path to the lost, or lighting a lamp in the dark so people with clear eyes can see what’s there, worthy Gotama has made the teaching clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the worthy Gotama, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. May I receive the going forth, the ordination in the worthy Gotama’s presence?” And the brahmin Bhāradvāja of Sundarikā received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence. And soon after, he became one of the perfected.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain. Then the student Māgha approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and said to the Buddha:
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 2.1)

“I’m a giver, worthy Gotama, a donor; I am bountiful and committed to charity. I seek wealth in a principled manner, and with that legitimate wealth I give to one person, to two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred people or even more. Giving and sacrificing like this, worthy Gotama, do I brim with much merit?”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 3.1)

“Indeed you do, student. A giver or donor who is bountiful and committed to charity, who seeks wealth in a principled manner, and with that legitimate wealth gives to one person, or up to a hundred people or even more, brims with much merit.” Then Māgha addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 4.1)

“I ask the bountiful Gotama,” said Māgha,
“wearing an ochre robe, wandering homeless.
Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity
makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit,
giving food and drink to others here:
how is their offering purified?”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 5.1)

“Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity,” replied the Buddha,
“makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit,
giving food and drink to others here:
such a one would succeed due to those who are worthy of donations.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 6.1)

“Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity,” said Māgha,
“makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit,
giving food and drink to others here:
explain to me who is worthy of donations.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 7.1)

“Those who wander the world unattached,
consummate, self-controlled, owning nothing:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 8.1)

Those who have cut off all fetters and bonds,
tamed, liberated, untroubled, with no need for hope:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 9.1)

Those who are released from all fetters,
tamed, liberated, untroubled, with no need for hope:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 10.1)

Having given up greed, hate, and delusion,
with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 11.1)

Those in whom dwells no deceit or conceit,
with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 12.1)

Those rid of greed, unselfish, with no need for hope,
with defilements ended, the spiritual journey completed:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 13.1)

Those not fallen prey to cravings,
who, having crossed the flood, live unselfishly:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 14.1)

Those with no craving at all in the world
for any state of existence in this life or the next:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 15.1)

Those who have left sensuality behind, wandering homeless,
self-controlled, straight as a shuttle:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 16.1)

Those freed of greed, with senses stilled,
like the moon released from the eclipse:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 17.1)

Those assuaged ones free of greed and anger,
for whom there are no destinies, being rid of them in this life:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 18.1)

They’ve given up rebirth and death completely,
and have gone beyond all indecision:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 19.1)

Those who live as their own island,
everywhere free, owning nothing:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 20.1)

Those here who know this to be true:
‘This is my last life, there are no future lives’:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 21.1)

A knowledge master, loving absorption, mindful,
who has reached awakening and is a refuge for many:
that is where a brahmin seeking merit
should bestow a timely oblation as sacrifice.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 22.1)

“Clearly my questions were not in vain!” said Māgha,
“The Buddha has explained to me who is worthy of donations.
You are the one here who knows this to be true,
for truly you understand this matter.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 23.1)

Suppose a lay donor who is committed to charity
makes a sacrifice seeking merit, looking for merit,
giving food and drink to others here:
explain to me how to accomplish the sacrifice.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 24.1)

“Sacrifice, and while doing so,” replied the Buddha,
“be clear and confident in every way.
Sacrifice is the ground standing upon which
the sacrificer sheds their flaws.
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 25.1)

One free of greed, rid of anger,
developing a heart of limitless love,
spreads that limitlessness in every direction,
ever diligent day and night.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 26.1)

“Who is purified, freed, awake?
How can one go to the realm of divinity oneself?
I do not know, so please tell me when asked,
for the Buddha is the divinity I see in person today!
To us you are truly the equal of divinity.
Brilliant One, how is one reborn in the realm of divinity?”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 27.1)

“One who accomplishes the sacrifice with three modes,” replied the Buddha,
“such a one would succeed due to those who are worthy of donations.
Sacrificing like this, one rightly committed to charity
is reborn in the realm of divinity, I say.”
With Māgha (Snp 3.5 28.1)

When he had spoken, the student Māgha said to the Buddha, “Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! … From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. Now at that time the wanderer Sabhiya had been presented with several questions by a deity who was a former blood relation, saying: “Sabhiya, you should live the spiritual life with whatever ascetic or brahmin answers these questions.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 2.1)

Then Sabhiya, after learning those questions in the presence of that deity, approached those ascetics and brahmins who led an order and a community, and taught a community, who were well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people. That is, Pūraṇa Kassapa, the bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, Ajita of the hair blanket, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and the Jain ascetic of the Ñātika clan. And he asked them those questions, but they were stumped by them. Displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness, they questioned Sabhiya in return.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 3.1)

Then Sabhiya thought, “Those famous ascetics and brahmins were stumped by my questions. Displaying annoyance, hate, and bitterness, they questioned me in return on that matter. Why don’t I return to a lesser life so I can enjoy sensual pleasures?”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 4.1)

Then Sabhiya thought, “This ascetic Gotama also leads an order and a community, and tutors a community. He’s a well-known and famous religious founder, deemed holy by many people. Why don’t I ask him these questions?”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 5.1)

Then he thought, “Even those ascetics and brahmins who are elderly and senior, who are advanced in years and have reached the final stage of life; who are senior, long standing, long gone forth; who lead an order and a community, and tutor a community; who are well-known and famous religious founders, deemed holy by many people—that is Pūraṇa Kassapa and the rest— were stumped by my questions. They displayed annoyance, hate, and bitterness, and even questioned me in return. How can the ascetic Gotama possibly answer my questions, since he is so young in age and newly gone forth?”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 6.1)

Then he thought, “An ascetic should not be looked down upon or disparaged because they are young. Though young, the ascetic Gotama has great psychic power and might. Why don’t I ask him these questions?”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 7.1)

Then Sabhiya set out for Rājagaha. Traveling stage by stage, he came to Rājagaha, the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. He went up to the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side, and addressed the Buddha in verse:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 8.1)

“I’ve come full of doubts and uncertainties,” said Sabhiya,
“wishing to ask some questions.
Please solve them for me.
Answer my questions in turn, in accordance with the truth.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 9.1)

“You have come from afar, Sabhiya,” said the Buddha,
“wishing to ask some questions.
I shall solve them for you,
answering your questions in turn, in accordance with the truth.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 10.1)

Ask me your question, Sabhiya,
whatever you want.
I’ll solve each and every
question you have.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 11.1)

Then Sabhiya thought, “Oh lord, how incredible, how amazing! Where those other ascetics and brahmins didn’t even give me a chance, the Buddha has invited me.” Uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, he asked this question.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 12.1)

“What must one attain to be called a mendicant?” said Sabhiya,
“How is one ‘gentle’, how said to be ‘tamed’?
How is one declared to be ‘awakened’?
May the Buddha please answer my question.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 13.1)

“When by the path they have walked themselves,” said the Buddha to Sabhiya,
“they reach extinguishment, with doubt overcome;
giving up desire for existence or nonexistence,
their journey complete, their rebirths ended: that is a mendicant.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 14.1)

Equanimous toward everything, mindful,
they don’t harm anyone in the world.
An ascetic who has crossed over, unclouded,
who has no pretensions, is gentle.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 15.1)

Their faculties have been developed
inside and out in the whole world.
Having pierced through this world and the next,
tamed, they await their time.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 16.1)

They have examined the eons in their entirety,
and both sides of transmigration—passing away and rebirth.
Rid of dust, unblemished, purified:
the one they call ‘awakened’ has attained the end of rebirth.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 17.1)
And then, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, Sabhiya asked another question:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 18.1)

“What must one attain to be called ‘brahmin’?” said Sabhiya.
“Why is one an ‘ascetic’, and how a ‘bathed initiate’?
How is one declared to be a ‘giant’?
May the Buddha please answer my question.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 19.1)

“Having banished all bad things,” said the Buddha to Sabhiya,
“immaculate, well-composed, steadfast,
consummate, they’ve left transmigration behind:
unattached, one such is called ‘brahmin’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 20.1)

An assuaged one who has given up good and evil,
stainless, understanding this world and the next,
gone beyond rebirth and death:
one such is rightly called ‘ascetic’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 21.1)

Having washed off all bad things
inside and out in the whole world,
among gods and humans bound to creations,
the one they call ‘washed’ does not return to creation.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 22.1)

They do nothing monstrous at all in the world,
discarding all yokes and bonds,
everywhere not stuck, freed:
one such is rightly called ‘giant’.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 23.1)
And then Sabhiya asked another question:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 24.1)

“Who is a ‘field-victor’ according to the Buddhas?” said Sabhiya,
“Why is one ‘skillful’, and how ‘an astute scholar’?
How is one declared to be a ‘sage’?
May the Buddha please answer my question.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 25.1)

“They are victors on the fields of deeds in their entirety,” said the Buddha to Sabhiya,
“the fields of gods, humans, and divinities;
released from the root bondage to all fields:
one such is rightly called ‘field-victor’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 26.1)

They have examined the coffers in their entirety,
the coffers of gods, humans, and divinities;
released from the root bondage to all coffers:
one such is rightly called ‘skillful’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 27.1)

They have examined whiteness
both inside and out; understanding purity,
they have left dark and bright behind:
one such is rightly called ‘an astute scholar’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 28.1)

Understanding the nature of the bad and the good
inside and out in the whole world;
one worthy of honor by gods and humans,
who has escaped from the net and the chain: that is a sage.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 29.1)
And then Sabhiya asked another question:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 30.1)

“What must one attain to be called ‘knowledge master’?” said Sabhiya,
“Why is one ‘studied’, and how is one ‘heroic’?
How to gain the name ‘thoroughbred’?
May the Buddha please answer my question.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 31.1)

“They have examined knowledges in their entirety,” said the Buddha to Sabhiya,
“those that are current among ascetics and brahmins;
rid of greed for all feelings,
having left all knowledges behind: that is a knowledge master.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 32.1)

Having studied proliferation and name & form
inside and out—the root of disease;
released from the root bondage to all disease:
one such is rightly called ‘studied’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 33.1)

Refraining from all evil here,
heroic, he escapes from the suffering of hell;
he is heroic and energetic:
one such is rightly called ‘hero’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 34.1)

Whoever’s bonds are cut,
the root of clinging inside and out;
released from the root bondage to all clinging:
one such is rightly called ‘thoroughbred’.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 35.1)
And then Sabhiya asked another question:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 36.1)

“What must one attain to be called ‘scholar’?” said Sabhiya,
“Why is one ‘noble’, and how is one ‘well conducted’?
How to gain the name ‘wanderer’?
May the Buddha please answer my question.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 37.1)

“One who has learned every teaching,” said the Buddha to Sabhiya,
“and has known for themselves what in the world is blameworthy and blameless;
a vanquisher, decided, liberated,
untroubled everywhere: they call them ‘scholar’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 38.1)

Having cut off defilements and clingings,
being wise, they enter no womb.
They’ve cast aside the bog of the three perceptions,
the one they call ‘noble’ does not return to creation.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 39.1)

One here who is accomplished and skillful in all forms of good conduct;
always understanding the teaching,
everywhere not stuck, freed in mind,
who has no aversion: they are ‘well-conducted’.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 40.1)

They wander full of wisdom,
having banished any deed that results in suffering,
deceit and conceit, as well as greed and anger,
above, below, all round, between.
They have made a limit on name and form;
the one they call a ‘wanderer’ has reached their destination.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 41.1)

And then, having approved and agreed with what the Buddha said, uplifted and elated, full of rapture and happiness, Sabhiya rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, raised his cupped palms toward the Buddha, and extolled the Buddha in his presence with fitting verses:
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 42.1)

“O one of vast wisdom, there are three and sixty opinions
based on the doctrines of ascetics:
they are expressions of perception, based on perception.
Having dispelled them all, you passed over the dark flood.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 43.1)

You have gone to the end, gone beyond suffering,
you are perfected, a fully awakened Buddha; I think you have ended defilements.
Brilliant, thoughtful, abounding in wisdom,
ender of suffering—you brought me across!
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 44.1)

When you understood my uncertainty,
you brought me beyond doubt—homage to you!
A sage, accomplished in the ways of sagacity,
you are gentle, not hardhearted, O Kinsman of the Sun.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 45.1)

Any doubts that I once had,
you have answered for me, O Clear-eyed One.
Clearly you are a sage, an Awakened One,
there are no hindrances in you.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 46.1)

All your distress
is blown away and mown down.
Cooled, tamed, steadfast:
truth is your strength.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 47.1)

O giant among giants, O great hero,
when you are speaking
all the gods rejoice,
including both Nārada and Pabbata.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 48.1)

Homage to you, O thoroughbred!
Homage to you, supreme among men!
In the world with its gods,
you have no rival.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 49.1)

You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher,
you are the sage who has overcome Māra;
you have cut off the underlying tendencies,
you’ve crossed over, and you bring humanity across.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 50.1)

You have transcended attachments,
your defilements are shattered;
you are a lion free of grasping,
with fear and dread given up.
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 51.1)

Like a graceful lotus
to which water does not stick,
so both good and evil
do not stick to you.
Stretch out your feet, great hero:
Sabhiya bows to the Teacher.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 52.1)

Then the wanderer Sabhiya bowed with his head to the Buddha’s feet and said, “Excellent, sir! Excellent! … I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the teaching, and to the mendicant Saṅgha. Sir, may I receive the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence?”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 53.1)

“Sabhiya, if someone formerly ordained in another sect wishes to take the going forth, the ordination in this teaching and training, they must spend four months on probation. When four months have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, they’ll give the going forth, the ordination into monkhood. However, I recognize individual differences in this matter.”
With Sabhiya (Snp 3.6 54.1)

“Sir, if four months probation are required in such a case, I’ll spend four years on probation. When four years have passed, if the mendicants are satisfied, let them give me the going forth, the ordination into monkhood.” And the wanderer Sabhiya received the going forth, the ordination in the Buddha’s presence. And Venerable Sabhiya became one of the perfected.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 1.1)

So I have heard. At one time the Buddha was wandering together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants in the land of the Aṅguttarāpans when he arrived at a town of theirs named Āpaṇa. The matted-hair ascetic Keṇiya heard: “It seems the ascetic Gotama—a Sakyan, gone forth from a Sakyan family—has arrived at Āpaṇa, together with a large Saṅgha of 1,250 mendicants. He has this good reputation: ‘That Blessed One is perfected, a fully awakened Buddha, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, holy, knower of the world, supreme guide for those fit for training, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ He has realized with his own insight this world—with its gods, Māras, and divinities, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, gods and humans—and he makes it known to others. He teaches Dhamma that’s good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well-phrased. And he reveals a spiritual practice that’s entirely full and pure. It’s good to see such perfected ones.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 2.1)

So Keṇiya approached the Buddha and exchanged greetings with him. When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side. The Buddha educated, encouraged, fired up, and inspired him with a Dhamma talk. Then he said to the Buddha, “Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?” When he said this, the Buddha said to him, “The Saṅgha is large, Keṇiya; there are 1,250 mendicants. And you are devoted to the brahmins.”
With Sela (Snp 3.7 3.1)

For a second time, Keṇiya asked the Buddha to accept a meal offering. “Never mind that the Saṅgha is large, with 1,250 mendicants, and that I am devoted to the brahmins. Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?” And for a second time, the Buddha gave the same reply.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 4.1)

For a third time, Keṇiya asked the Buddha to accept a meal offering. “Never mind that the Saṅgha is large, with 1,250 mendicants, and that I am devoted to the brahmins. Would Worthy Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha please accept tomorrow’s meal from me?” The Buddha consented with silence. Then, knowing that the Buddha had consented, Keṇiya rose from his seat and went to his own hermitage. There he addressed his friends and colleagues, relatives and kin, “My friends and colleagues, relatives and kin: please listen! The ascetic Gotama together with the mendicant Saṅgha has been invited by me for tomorrow’s meal. Please help me out with the manual preparations.” “Yes, worthy sir,” they replied. Some dug ovens, some chopped wood, some washed dishes, some set up a water jar, and some spread out seats. Meanwhile, Keṇiya set up the pavilion himself.
With Sela (Snp 3.7 5.1)

Now at that time the brahmin Sela was residing in Āpaṇa. He had mastered the three Vedas, together with their vocabularies and ritual performance, their phonology and word classification, and the testaments as fifth. He knew them word-by-word, and their grammar. He was well versed in cosmology and the marks of a great man. And he was teaching three hundred young students to recite the hymns.
